newsitem.title: TURKEY: Anti-Islamist army puts strain on Turkey coalition.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Islamist army puts strain on Turkey coalition.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led coalition strained at the seams on Friday in the shadow of secularist generals angered by Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's reluctance to curb a Moslem religious upsurge.

Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey, held almost two hours of hastily arranged talks with his pro-Western government ally Tansu Ciller amid reports the alliance was near to imploding under military pressure.
The pair left the prime minister's office separately after the meeting without making any comment to waiting reporters.
Armed forces chief Ismail Hakki Karadayi said the army would keep out of politics, despite its public opposition to Erbakan that has set the coalition's two wings against each other.
"The Turkish armed forces exist completely outside politics and they will stay outside," state-run Anatolian new agency quoted Karadayi as saying.
He warned, however, that the soldiers were upset at what they see as Islamist attempts to force religion on all walks of life and scrap Turkey's secular system.

"There are some developments in our country against the basic constitutional properties of our republic to which our people and our armed forces are extremely sensitive," he said. "Nobody can remain insensible and impartial in the face of this. But the place to resolve this is parliament."
The top brass is expected to confront Erbakan at a National Security Council meeting on Saturday with his failure to carry out an anti-Islamist crackdown demanded by the army months ago.

Two anti-Islamist ministers from Ciller's wing are in open rebellion against Erbakan's Welfare Party for stalling on military plans to restrict religious education, penalise Islamist dress and move against Islamist business and media.
Ciller earlier denied a press story that she would pull out of the alliance to keep her party together.
"Don't believe things about withdrawing from the government that you haven't heard from me," she told reporters after an unscheduled leadership meeting of her True Path Party (DYP).
Turkish stocks were little changed after falling nearly five percent on Thursday over political worries. The main Istanbul index closed up 0.62 percent.
An Islamist cabinet member acknowledged all was not well between the coalition partners.
"It's not a piece of cake but we can hardly say either that everything is over, that the government has gone," State Minister Mehmet Altinsoy told Reuters.

A war of attrition between Welfare and the army reached a new height on Thursday when the Islamists threatened legal action against a middle-ranking general who had verbally abused Erbakan in comments seen on national television.
The commander called Erbakan a "pimp" for going on pilgrimage to the Moslem holy city of Mecca as the guest of conservative Saudi King Fahd.

Military sources said the exact agenda for Saturday's meeting was not clear yet but the Turkish media has reported that an army demand to extend secularist education to eight years from the current five would be debated.
A spokesman for Ciller's party was confident Erbakan's faction would eventually back the eight-year plan, despite opposition from his grassroots.
"The matter of eight years' education will be put to parliament by the government," leading True Path member Hasan Ekinci told a news conference.
The planned education reforms would marginalise religious secondary schools seen as producing the next breed of Islamists.
Generals have ousted three governments since 1960 but observers say they army is reluctant to stage another coup partly because it would badly damage NATO member Turkey's bid to get closer to Europe.

The army is practically the only state authority in a large chunk of southeastern Turkey where troops are fighting Kurdish separatist rebels. Turkey also keeps some 30,000 troops on the divided island of Cyprus.
